stem:
What does `K` resolve to?

```ts
type K = keyof { a: 1; b: 2 };
```

options.why: `keyof` produces a union of the property names as string literal types.
That is the union of the property value types, which is `T[keyof T]`, not `keyof T`.

options.text: `string`
options.why: `keyof` keeps the exact literal names; it only widens to `string` for a string index signature.
`keyof` produces a union, never a tuple. TypeScript has no built-in way to get keys as an ordered tuple.

explanation: `keyof T` is the union of the known property keys of `T` as literal types. For `{ a: 1; b: 2 }` that is `"a" | "b"`. To get the value types instead, index with that union: `T[keyof T]` gives `1 | 2`.

stem: Given `interface User { id: number; name: string }`, which declaration compiles under `strict`?

options.text: `const b: Partial<User> = { id: "1" };` because Partial loosens the property types too
options.why: Partial only adds `?` to each property; `id` must still be a number when present.

options.text: `const a: Partial<User> = {};`
options.why: Every property of `Partial<User>` is optional, so an empty object is a valid value.

options.text: `const c: Partial<User> = { id: 1, age: 3 };` because extra keys are allowed
options.why: Object literals still get excess property checks, and `age` is not a property of User.

options.text: `const d: Partial<User> = null;` because every property may be missing
options.why: Partial makes properties optional, not the whole object nullable. Under strictNullChecks null is rejected.

explanation: `Partial<T>` is `{ [K in keyof T]?: T[K] }`. It makes each property optional and changes nothing else: the property types, the excess-property check on literals and nullability of the whole value all stay the same.

stem: With `type R = Readonly<{ pos: { x: number } }>` and `declare const r: R`, the statement `r.pos.x = 1;` is a compile error.

options.text: True
options.why: It looks protected, but `Readonly` only marks the top-level property `pos` as readonly.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: `Readonly` is shallow. `r.pos = …` errors, but `r.pos.x = 1` compiles because the inner object is still mutable.

explanation: `Readonly<T>` is `{ readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] }`, a single mapped layer. Reassigning `r.pos` is rejected with "Cannot assign to 'pos' because it is a read-only property", but the nested object type `{ x: number }` is unchanged, so its fields can still be written. For deep immutability you need a recursive type or `as const` on a literal.

stem:
What is `Pick<User, "id" | "name">`?

```ts
type User = { id: number; name: string; email: string };
```

options.text: `{ email: string }`, because Pick removes the listed keys
options.why: That describes `Omit<User, "id" | "name">`. Pick keeps the listed keys.

options.text: `"id" | "name"`, the union of the selected key names
options.why: Pick returns an object type, not a union of keys.

options.text: `{ id: number; name: string }`
options.why: Pick builds a new object type with only the listed properties and their original types.

options.text: `{ id?: number; name?: string }`, because picked keys become optional
options.why: Pick copies each property with its original modifiers; it does not add `?`.

explanation: `Pick<T, K extends keyof T>` is `{ [P in K]: T[P] }`. It keeps exactly the keys you list, with their original types and modifiers. Its counterpart `Omit<T, K>` keeps everything except the listed keys.

stem:
Type the union that this resolves to.

```ts
type T = Exclude<"a" | "b" | "c", "a">;
```
explanation: `Exclude<T, U>` is `T extends U ? never : T`, a distributive conditional type. It checks each member of the union separately: `"a"` is removed, while `"b"` and `"c"` are kept, giving `"b" | "c"`.

stem:
What happens when this compiles?

```ts
const pages: Record<"home" | "about", string> = { home: "/" };
```

options.text: It compiles, because Record keys are optional by default
options.why: Record makes every key in its union required. Use `Partial<Record<…>>` for optional keys.

options.text: Error: property `about` is missing
options.why: `Record<"home" | "about", string>` is `{ home: string; about: string }`, so both keys are required.

options.text: Error: Record only accepts `string` as its key type
options.why: Any subtype of `string | number | symbol` works as a key type, including literal unions.

options.text: It compiles, but `pages.about` has type `string | undefined`
options.why: The literal never reaches that point: the missing key is already a compile error at the declaration.

explanation: `Record<K, V>` is `{ [P in K]: V }`. With a union of literal keys it produces one required property per key, so omitting `about` gives "Property 'about' is missing in type '{ home: string; }'". This makes Record a handy exhaustiveness check for lookup tables.

stem:
Which type is `"port" | "host"`?

```ts
const config = { port: 3000, host: "localhost" };
```

options.text: `keyof config`, since keyof works on values as well as types
options.why: `keyof` only accepts types. Writing `keyof config` is an error because `config` is a value.

options.text: `typeof keyof config`, which reads the keys first and then takes their type
options.why: That is not valid syntax: `typeof` must be followed by a value expression, not a type operator.

options.text: `keyof typeof config`
options.why: `typeof config` turns the value into its type, and `keyof` then lists that type's keys.

options.text: `typeof config[keyof config]`, which indexes the object by every key
options.why: That mixes a value with a type operator, and indexing would give value types, not key names.

explanation: Type operators work on types, so reach for a value's type first: `typeof config` is `{ port: number; host: string }`, and `keyof typeof config` is `"port" | "host"`. This pattern keeps key unions in sync with a runtime object automatically.

stem: Match each utility type with what it produces from `T`.

options.text: Every property becomes optional
options.why: This is what Partial does.

options.text: Every property becomes required, with `?` removed
options.why: This is what Required does.

options.text: Every top-level property becomes readonly
options.why: This is what Readonly does.

options.text: `null` and `undefined` are removed from a union
options.why: This is what NonNullable does.

explanation: Partial, Required and Readonly are mapped types that change property modifiers (`?` and `readonly`). NonNullable is different: it works on a union type, keeping every member except `null` and `undefined`, so `NonNullable<string | null | undefined>` is `string`.

stem:
What is `ReturnType<typeof makeResult>`?

```ts
const makeResult = () => ({ ok: true });
```

options.text: `{ ok: true }`, since the literal value true is kept
options.why: Without `as const`, the property in a returned object literal is widened from `true` to `boolean`.

options.text: `{ ok: boolean }`
options.why: The function's inferred return type widens the literal, and ReturnType reads that inferred type.

options.text: `() => { ok: boolean }`, the type of the whole function
options.why: That is `typeof makeResult`. ReturnType extracts just the return type.

options.text: An error, because ReturnType only works on declared function types
options.why: ReturnType works on any function type, including one taken from a value with `typeof`.

explanation: `ReturnType<typeof fn>` reads the function's return type as TypeScript inferred it. Mutable object properties widen literals, so `true` becomes `boolean`. Returning `{ ok: true } as const` would give `{ readonly ok: true }` instead.

options.text: `number`, because indexed access ignores the optional modifier
options.why: Under strict mode an optional property's read type includes `undefined`, and indexed access reflects that.

options.text: `number | undefined`
options.why: Indexed access types chain like property reads, and `zip` is optional.

options.text: An error, because you can only index one level deep
options.why: Indexed access types can be chained to any depth, just like property access on values.

options.text: `{ zip?: number }`, the slice of the object that contains zip
options.why: Indexed access returns the property's type, not an object containing it. That would be `Pick`.

explanation: `T["k"]` reads the type of property `k`, and you can chain it: `Order["shipping"]` is `{ city: string; zip?: number }`, and then `["zip"]` is `number | undefined`. With `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` off (the default), optional properties carry `undefined` in their type.

stem: Given `interface Todo { title: string; done: boolean; due?: Date }`, which two types make `due` a required property? (Choose two.)

options.text: `Required<Todo>`
options.why: Required removes the `?` from every property, including `due`.

options.text: `Todo & { due: Date }`
options.why: In an intersection a property is optional only if it is optional in every member, so `due` becomes required.

options.text: `Partial<Todo>`
options.why: Partial makes every property optional, which is the opposite.

options.text: `Readonly<Todo>`
options.why: Readonly adds `readonly` but keeps `due` optional.

options.text: `Pick<Todo, "due">`
options.why: Pick keeps each property's original modifiers, so `due` stays optional.

explanation: Two common ways to tighten an optional property: `Required<T>` strips `?` from all properties, and intersecting with `{ due: Date }` overrides just one. Pick, Readonly and other homomorphic mapped types copy the original modifiers unless they explicitly change them.

options.text: `string`, because the index signature is declared with string keys
options.why: It is wider than that: numeric keys are also allowed, since JavaScript converts them to strings.

options.text: `never`, because the interface has no named properties at all
options.why: An index signature contributes key types to `keyof` even without named properties.

options.text: `PropertyKey`, because any key at all can be used to index the object
options.why: Symbols are not covered by a string index signature, so `symbol` is not part of the result.

options.text: `string | number`
options.why: A string index signature also accepts numeric keys, because `obj[1]` is the same as `obj["1"]` in JavaScript.

explanation: For a type with a string index signature, `keyof` is `string | number`: numbers are allowed because JavaScript converts numeric property keys to strings. A quirk to know: `keyof Record<string, number>` reports just `string`, because `keyof` a mapped type `{ [P in K]: V }` returns its constraint `K` directly, even though both types accept the same keys.

options.text: Both lines are errors, because the key must exist in User
options.why: Only Pick constrains its keys to `keyof T`. Omit is declared with `K extends keyof any`.

options.text: Both lines compile, and both produce an empty object type
options.why: Pick rejects the unknown key: "Type '"nmae"' does not satisfy the constraint 'keyof User'".

options.text: `A` compiles silently and still contains `name`; `B` is an error
options.why: Omit accepts any key, so the typo removes nothing, while Pick checks that the key exists.

options.text: `A` is an error, while `B` compiles and produces `{}`
options.why: It is the other way round: Pick is the strict one.

explanation: The lib defines `Pick<T, K extends keyof T>` but `Omit<T, K extends keyof any>`. Omit's looser constraint lets it work with keys that may not exist, but it also means a typo silently omits nothing. Teams that want a strict version define `type StrictOmit<T, K extends keyof T> = Omit<T, K>`.

stem:
What does `M<{ a?: number; readonly b: number }>` resolve to?

```ts
type M<T> = { [K in keyof T]: string };
```

options.text: `{ a: string; b: string }`, since a mapped type starts from scratch
options.why: A mapped type over `keyof T` is homomorphic and copies the modifiers of each original property.

options.text: `{ a?: string; readonly b: string }`
options.why: Homomorphic mapped types keep `?` and `readonly` from the source properties.

options.text: `{ a?: string | undefined; b: string }`, keeping `?` but dropping readonly
options.why: Both modifiers are copied. Only explicit `-readonly` or `-?` removes them.

options.text: `{ a: string | undefined; readonly b: string }`, with `?` turned into undefined
options.why: The property stays optional; it is not converted into a required property with undefined.

explanation: A mapped type of the form `{ [K in keyof T]: … }` is called homomorphic. It keeps the optional and readonly modifiers of each property in `T`. That is why `Partial`, `Readonly` and `Pick` preserve modifiers they do not explicitly change. To change modifiers, write them explicitly with `+` or `-`.

stem: Which definition of `Mutable<T>` turns `{ readonly a: 1; readonly b?: 2 }` into `{ a: 1; b?: 2 }`?

options.text: `type Mutable<T> = { -readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] };`
options.why: The `-readonly` modifier removes readonly, and being homomorphic it keeps `b` optional.

options.text: `type Mutable<T> = { [K in keyof T]: T[K] };`, since mapping drops readonly
options.why: A plain homomorphic mapped type copies `readonly`, so nothing changes.

options.text: `type Mutable<T> = { readonly [K in keyof T]-?: T[K] };` to flip the flags
options.why: That adds readonly and also removes `?`, the opposite of what is wanted.

options.text: `type Mutable<T> = Omit<T, "readonly">;` to strip the modifier key
options.why: `readonly` is a modifier, not a property key, so Omit has nothing to remove.

explanation: Mapping modifiers take an optional `+` or `-` prefix. `-readonly` removes the readonly flag and `-?` removes optionality. Without a prefix, a homomorphic mapped type copies modifiers unchanged. TypeScript ships `Readonly` but no built-in `Mutable`, so this one-liner is a common interview question.

stem:
What is `T`?

```ts
type T = Exclude<string | number | (() => void), Function>;
```

options.text: `never`, because a primitive cannot be compared with Function
options.why: Exclude checks each member separately; primitives are simply not assignable to Function, so they stay.

options.text: `string | number | (() => void)`, since Function is an interface
options.why: Function types are assignable to the global `Function` interface, so the function member is removed.

options.text: `string | number`
options.why: Exclude distributes over the union and drops only the member assignable to Function.

options.text: `() => void`, keeping only the member that matches Function
options.why: That is what `Extract` does. Exclude keeps the members that do not match.

explanation: `Exclude<T, U>` is `T extends U ? never : T`. Because `T` is a naked type parameter, the conditional distributes: each union member is tested on its own. `() => void` is assignable to `Function` and becomes `never`; `string` and `number` are kept.

stem: What is `Awaited<Promise<Promise<number>>>`?

options.text: `Promise<number>`, because Awaited unwraps only one level
options.why: Awaited is recursive, which matches how `await` flattens nested promises at runtime.

options.text: `number`
options.why: Awaited keeps unwrapping thenables until it reaches a non-promise type.

options.text: `Promise<Promise<number>>`, since nested promises cannot be unwrapped
options.why: Nested promises can be unwrapped; that is exactly the job Awaited was added for in TypeScript 4.5.

options.text: `unknown`, because the inner type is lost at the second level
options.why: The inner type is fully preserved, so the result is precise.

explanation: `Awaited<T>` models what `await` does: it recursively unwraps any thenable until it reaches a value type. At runtime a promise can never resolve to another promise, so the type of `await p` for `Promise<Promise<number>>` is `number`. `Promise.all` and async function return types use Awaited internally.

stem:
What is `Parameters<typeof send>[2]`?

```ts
function send(to: string, body: { text: string }, retries = 3) {}
```

options.text: `number`, the type of the default value
options.why: Callers can omit the argument, so the parameter type seen from outside includes `undefined`.

options.text: `3`, the literal default value
options.why: Defaults do not create literal types: the parameter is widened to `number`.

options.text: `number | undefined`
options.why: A parameter with a default is optional, so its slot in the Parameters tuple is `number | undefined`.

options.text: `{ text: string }`, because tuple indexes start at 1
options.why: Tuple indexes start at 0, so `[2]` is the third parameter, `retries`.

explanation: `Parameters<F>` returns the parameter list as a tuple, here `[to: string, body: { text: string }, retries?: number]`. A parameter with a default is optional from the caller's side, so indexing the optional element gives `number | undefined`. Indexing with `[1]` would give `{ text: string }`.

stem: Given `type RA = Record<string, number>` and `interface RB { [key: string]: number }`, which two statements are true under default `strict` settings? (Choose two.)

options.text: Values of `RA` and `RB` are assignable to each other in both directions
options.why: Both describe an object whose string keys all map to numbers, so they are structurally equivalent.

options.text: Reading `ra.anything` has type `number`, with no `undefined` added
options.why: Without `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, index signature reads are assumed to hit a value.

options.text: `const r: RA = { x: 1, y: "two" }` compiles, because Record values are not checked
options.why: Every value must be a number, so `"two"` is rejected.

options.text: `Record<string, number>` requires at least one key, so `{}` is not assignable
options.why: An empty object satisfies an index signature: it simply has no keys.

options.text: `RB` can also declare a property `name: string` next to its index signature
options.why: Named properties must be compatible with the string index signature's value type, `number`.

explanation: `Record<string, number>` maps over `string` and produces an index signature, so it behaves like `{ [key: string]: number }`. Index signature reads are unsound by default: `ra.missing` is typed `number` even though it is `undefined` at runtime. Turn on `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` to get `number | undefined` instead. Named properties in an interface with a string index signature must fit the index signature's type.

stem: Given `type U = "a" | "b" | 1`, which two types evaluate to exactly `"a" | "b"`? (Choose two.)

options.text: `Extract<U, string>`
options.why: Extract keeps the members assignable to `string`: `"a"` and `"b"`.

options.text: `Exclude<U, number>`
options.why: Exclude drops the member assignable to `number`, which is `1`.

options.text: `NonNullable<U>`
options.why: U contains no null or undefined, so NonNullable leaves all three members.

options.text: `Extract<U, number>`
options.why: That keeps only the numeric member, giving `1`.

options.text: `Omit<U, 1>`
options.why: Omit works on object properties. Applied to a union of primitives it produces an object type made of their shared members, not a filtered union.

explanation: `Extract<T, U>` keeps union members assignable to `U`, and `Exclude<T, U>` removes them. Both distribute over the union. `Omit` and `Pick` operate on object keys and are the wrong tools for filtering unions of literals.

Without `as const`, the array literal is inferred as `(string | number | boolean)[]`: each element is widened and merged into one element type. Indexing an array type with `number` gives its element type, so `Item` is `string | number | boolean`. With `as const` the result would be `1 | "a" | true`.

stem: Order these types from the widest (accepts the most values) to the narrowest.

options.why: A single literal type, the narrowest here.

options.text: `PropertyKey`
options.why: string | number | symbol, the widest here.

options.text: `string`
options.why: All strings.
Two string literals.

options.text: `string | number`
options.why: All strings plus all numbers.

explanation: `PropertyKey` is the built-in alias for `string | number | symbol` (the same as `keyof any`). Removing `symbol` gives `string | number`, then `string`, then a union of two literals, then a single literal. Each type is assignable to every type before it in this order.

stem: Given `type Cat = { name: string; meow(): void }` and `type Dog = { name: string; bark(): void }`, the type `Pick<Cat | Dog, "meow">` compiles.

options.text: True
options.why: It would only compile if every member of the union had `meow`.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: `keyof (Cat | Dog)` is only the shared key `"name"`, so `"meow"` fails Pick's `K extends keyof T` constraint.

explanation: A value of type `Cat | Dog` is only guaranteed to have the keys common to both members, so `keyof (Cat | Dog)` is `"name"`. The compiler reports "Type '"meow"' does not satisfy the constraint '"name"'". To pick from each member separately, use a distributive helper such as `T extends any ? Pick<T, …> : never`.

stem: Given `type T = { a: string; b: number }` and `type Tup = [boolean, string]`, match each type expression with its result.

options.text: `string`
options.why: The type of property a.

options.text: `string | number`
options.why: The union of all property value types.
The union of the keys.

options.text: `boolean | string`
options.why: The union of the tuple element types.

explanation: Indexed access with a single key reads one property; indexing with a union of keys (`keyof T`) gives the union of their value types. `keyof T` itself is the union of key names. Indexing a tuple or array with `number` yields the union of its element types.

options.text: `"a" | "b" | "c"` for the union and `"c"` for the intersection
options.why: That is reversed. A union value only promises the shared keys; an intersection value has all of them.

options.text: `"c"` for the union and `"a" | "b" | "c"` for the intersection
options.why: keyof of a union is the intersection of the keys, and keyof of an intersection is the union of the keys.

options.text: `"a" | "b" | "c"` for both
options.why: For the union, TypeScript cannot know whether the value is an A or a B, so only `c` is safe.

options.text: `never` for the union and `"c"` for the intersection
options.why: The union still shares `c`, and the intersection has every key from both types.

explanation: The rule flips: `keyof (A | B)` is `keyof A & keyof B` (keys present in every member), and `keyof (A & B)` is `keyof A | keyof B` (keys present in any member). This matters when writing generic helpers over unions, which often need distribution to reach member-specific keys.

options.text: `Omit` cannot remove a key that appears in more than one member; remove `id` from each type by hand
options.why: Omit removes shared keys fine. The problem is what happens to the keys that are not shared.

options.text: The discriminant was renamed by Omit; add `kind` back with an intersection to restore narrowing
options.why: `kind` survives, but as `"circle" | "square"` on a single object type, so narrowing has nothing to split.

options.text: `Omit` is not distributive, giving `{ kind: "circle" | "square" }`; use `T extends any ? Omit<T, K> : never`
options.why: Omit maps over `keyof (Circle | Square)`, the shared keys only, so member-specific fields are lost.

options.text: The result is correct but needs `as const` on the objects so that TypeScript narrows them again
options.why: The type itself has lost `radius` and `side`; no annotation on values brings them back.

explanation: `Omit<T, K>` is `Pick<T, Exclude<keyof T, K>>`. For a union, `keyof T` is only the shared keys (`kind` and `id`), so the result collapses into one object `{ kind: "circle" | "square" }`. A distributive version applies Omit to each member: `type DistributiveOmit<T, K extends PropertyKey> = T extends any ? Omit<T, K> : never`, which keeps the union and its discriminant.

options.text: `{ a: string; b: never; c: "x" }`, keeping b but typing it as never
options.why: Remapping a key to `never` removes the property entirely; it does not keep it with a never type.

options.text: `{ a: string }`, because `"x"` is a literal and not the string type
options.why: A string literal type is assignable to `string`, so `c` passes the check.

options.text: `{}`, because the `as` clause filters on keys, not on their value types
options.why: The `as` clause can use `T[K]`, so filtering by value type works.

options.text: `{ a: string; c: "x" }`
options.why: Keys whose value type extends string are kept; `b` is remapped to `never` and dropped.

explanation: Key remapping with `as` (TypeScript 4.1) computes a new key for each property. If the new key is `never`, the property is filtered out. Here `T[K] extends string` is true for `string` and for `"x"`, and false for `number`, so the result keeps `a` and `c`.
reference: TypeScript Handbook: Key Remapping via as

options.text: To force TypeScript to evaluate keys eagerly instead of lazily
options.why: Evaluation order is not the issue; it is a constraint error.

options.text: `keyof T` may include `number` and `symbol`, but `Capitalize` only accepts string types
options.why: Intersecting with `string` keeps only string keys, which satisfies Capitalize's constraint.

options.text: Without it, numeric keys would be capitalised into a different case and collide
options.why: Numbers have no case. Without the intersection the code does not compile at all.

options.text: It turns the keys into template literal types so that the remapped names autocomplete
options.why: Plain `K` would be an error: "Type 'K' does not satisfy the constraint 'string'".

explanation: `keyof T` is typed as `string | number | symbol` in general, while intrinsic string types such as `Capitalize<S extends string>` require a string. `string & K` keeps the string keys and turns symbol or number keys into `never`, which also drops them from the result. With `{ name: string; age: number }` this yields `{ getName: () => string; getAge: () => number }`.

stem:
What is `Box<[number, string]>`?

```ts
type Box<T> = { [K in keyof T]: { v: T[K] } };
```

options.text: An object with keys "0", "1", "length", "push" and every other array member boxed
options.why: That happens only when mapping over the keys of a concrete tuple type, not through a type parameter.

options.text: `{ v: number | string }[]`, because mapped types turn tuples into arrays
options.why: Homomorphic mapped types preserve tuple-ness, including length and element positions.

options.text: `[{ v: number }, { v: string }]`
options.why: A homomorphic mapped type instantiated with a tuple maps each element and returns a tuple.

options.text: An error, because `keyof` cannot be used on a tuple type parameter
options.why: `keyof` works on tuples, and mapped types have special handling for them.

explanation: When a homomorphic mapped type `{ [K in keyof T]: … }` is instantiated with an array or tuple type for `T`, TypeScript maps only the element types and produces an array or tuple of the same shape. This is how `Partial<[a, b]>` gives `[a?, b?]` and `Readonly<string[]>` gives `readonly string[]`.
reference: TypeScript 3.1 release notes: Mapped types on tuples and arrays

stem: Using the naive definition `type DeepReadonly<T> = { readonly [K in keyof T]: DeepReadonly<T[K]> }`, the call `dr.f()` compiles when `dr` has type `DeepReadonly<{ f: () => void }>`.

options.text: True
options.why: It looks harmless, but mapping over a function type keeps only its properties, not its call signature.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: `DeepReadonly<() => void>` becomes `{}`, which has no call signature, so `dr.f()` is an error.

explanation: A mapped type iterates over properties. A function type like `() => void` has no properties of its own, so mapping over it yields an object type without a call signature, and the compiler reports "This expression is not callable". Production DeepReadonly types stop at functions, for example with `T extends (...args: any[]) => any ? T : …`. Primitives are fine: a homomorphic mapped type returns primitives unchanged.

stem: What is `Partial<{ a: 1 } | { b: 2 }>`?

options.text: `{ a?: 1; b?: 2 }`, a single object merging both members
options.why: Mapped types do not merge union members into one object.
Homomorphic mapped types distribute over a union passed as their type parameter.

options.text: `{}`, because the two members share no keys
options.why: That would be true of mapping over `keyof (A | B)` directly, but Partial is applied member by member.

options.text: An error, because Partial cannot take a union type
options.why: Any object type, including a union, is a valid argument.

explanation: When a homomorphic mapped type such as `Partial<T>` receives a union for `T`, it is applied to each member separately and the results are unioned. This is why `Partial` keeps discriminated unions intact, unlike `Omit`, which is built on `keyof` of the whole union.

stem: Which two statements about `Readonly<string[]>` are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: It is the same type as `readonly string[]`
options.why: A homomorphic mapped type applied to an array type produces the corresponding readonly array type.

options.text: Calling `.push("x")` on a value of this type is a compile error
options.why: `ReadonlyArray` has no mutating methods, so push does not exist on it.

options.text: A value of this type can be assigned to a variable of type `string[]`
options.why: Readonly arrays are not assignable to mutable ones: "The type 'readonly string[]' is 'readonly' and cannot be assigned to the mutable type 'string[]'".

options.text: It produces an object with readonly numeric keys but keeps `push`
options.why: Mapped types over arrays are special-cased to produce `ReadonlyArray`, which has no push.

options.text: It freezes the array at runtime, like `Object.freeze`
options.why: Types are erased at compile time. Readonly has no runtime effect.

explanation: `Readonly<T>` on an array becomes `readonly T[]`, an alias for `ReadonlyArray<T>`, which omits mutating methods such as push, pop and sort. Assignability is one way: `string[]` is assignable to `readonly string[]`, but not the reverse. None of this exists at runtime.

options.text: `ReturnType<typeof parse>` is `string`
options.why: For overloaded functions, inference from the type uses the last overload signature.

options.text: `Parameters<typeof parse>` is `[x: number]`
options.why: Parameters also reads only the last overload.

options.text: `ReturnType<typeof parse>` is `number | string`
options.why: TypeScript does not merge overloads into a union when inferring from a function type.

options.text: `ReturnType<typeof parse>` is `any`, taken from the implementation signature
options.why: The implementation signature is not visible to callers or to `typeof`.

options.text: `ReturnType<typeof parse>` is `number`, from the first overload
options.why: Inference picks the last overload, not the first.

explanation: Utilities such as `ReturnType` and `Parameters` are conditional types using `infer`. When the source type has several call signatures, inference uses the last one (the most general by convention). The implementation signature is hidden from the outside. To get all variants, model the function as an overloaded type or a union of function types yourself.
reference: TypeScript Handbook: Inferring Within Conditional Types

stem:
Type what this resolves to.

```ts
type L = Parameters<(a: string, b?: number) => void>["length"];
```
explanation: `Parameters` gives the tuple `[a: string, b?: number]`. A tuple with an optional element can have either length, so its `length` property is the union `1 | 2`. A tuple with no optional or rest elements has a single literal length, and a rest element makes it `number`.

stem: Put the steps in order that TypeScript takes when it evaluates `Omit<User, "id">`, based on its definition in the standard library.

options.text: Run `Pick<User, …>` with the remaining keys
options.why: Pick builds the final object type.

options.text: Compute `keyof User`
options.why: Omit first needs every key of User.

options.text: Copy each kept property with its original modifiers
options.why: Pick is homomorphic, so `?` and readonly survive.

options.text: Apply `Exclude<…, "id">` to remove the omitted key from that union
options.why: Exclude distributes over the key union.

explanation: The lib defines `type Omit<T, K extends keyof any> = Pick<T, Exclude<keyof T, K>>`. So TypeScript computes `keyof User`, removes `"id"` with a distributive Exclude, and passes the remaining keys to Pick, which maps over them and copies each property's type and modifiers.

stem: Given `type T = { readonly a?: number }`, match each mapped type with its result.

options.text: `{ a: number }`
options.why: readonly removed, `?` removed.

options.text: `{ readonly a: number }`
options.why: Only `?` removed.

options.text: `{ a?: number }`
options.why: Only readonly removed.

options.text: `{ readonly a?: number }`
options.why: Modifiers copied unchanged.

explanation: A homomorphic mapped type copies `readonly` and `?` unless you change them. A `-` prefix removes a modifier and `+` (or no sign, when written) adds it. When `-?` removes optionality it also removes the `undefined` that came from the `?`, which is why the results show plain `number`.

stem:
What is `Concrete<{ a?: number | undefined; b: string | undefined }>`?

```ts
type Concrete<T> = { [K in keyof T]-?: T[K] };
```

options.text: `{ a: number | undefined; b: string | undefined }`, since -? only touches the modifier
options.why: For a property that was optional, removing `?` also strips `undefined` from its type.

options.text: `{ a: number; b: string }`, since -? strips undefined from every property
options.why: `b` was never optional, so its explicit `undefined` is left alone.

options.text: `{ a: number; b: string | undefined }`
options.why: `-?` removes `undefined` only from properties that were optional; `b` keeps its declared union.

options.text: `{ a?: number; b: string }`, because -? applies only to required properties
options.why: `-?` removes optionality, so `a` becomes required.

explanation: When `-?` makes an optional property required, TypeScript also removes `undefined` from its type, since the `undefined` is assumed to come from the optionality (this is how `Required<T>` behaves). It does not touch required properties, so `b: string | undefined` is copied as is. With `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` on, an explicit `| undefined` on an optional property is treated as part of the declared type.

options.text: `2`, because mapping a tuple keeps its length
options.why: Tuple shape is preserved only when the mapped type is instantiated through a type parameter.

options.text: `boolean`
options.why: Mapping over the keys of a concrete tuple type maps every member, including length and push, to boolean.

options.text: `number`, because length is not part of keyof a tuple
options.why: `keyof [number, string]` includes "0", "1", "length" and every array method name.

options.text: An error, because tuples cannot be used in a mapped type at all
options.why: The mapped type is valid; it just treats the tuple as an ordinary object type.

explanation: The special tuple-and-array handling applies to homomorphic mapped types whose `keyof T` refers to a type parameter, such as `Box<T>` instantiated with a tuple. Here `keyof [number, string]` is evaluated directly, giving a union of every key ("0", "1", "length", "push", "map" and so on), and each one maps to `boolean`. So `c.length` is `boolean` and `c[0]` is `boolean` too.
reference: TypeScript 3.1 release notes: Mapped types on tuples and arrays

options.text: `string`, because only `id` is removed and `name` keeps its declared type
options.why: With a string index signature, `keyof Props` is `string | number`, and the named keys are absorbed into it.

options.text: An error, because `name` no longer exists on the result
options.why: The result still has a string index signature, so reading `name` is allowed.

options.text: `unknown`
options.why: The known properties are lost: Omit rebuilds the type from the index signature alone.

options.text: `string | unknown`, a union of the named and index types
options.why: `string | unknown` would collapse to `unknown` anyway, but the real reason is that `name` itself was dropped.

explanation: `keyof Props` is `string | number`: the literal keys `"id"` and `"name"` are subsumed by `string`. `Exclude<string | number, "id">` cannot remove a literal from `string`, so Pick maps over `string | number` and produces `{ [x: string]: unknown; [x: number]: unknown }`. Every named property is lost. To keep them, first strip the index signature with key remapping, then Omit.
reference: TypeScript Handbook: Index Signatures; Utility Types (Omit)

stem: Which type removes the index signature from `interface P { [k: string]: unknown; id: number; name: string }` and leaves exactly `{ id: number; name: string }`?

options.text: `{ [K in keyof T as K extends string ? K : never]: T[K] }`, keeping only the string keys
options.why: The index signature key `string` also extends string, so it survives the filter.

options.text: `Omit<T, string>`, which removes every string key
options.why: That removes all string keys, including `id` and `name`, leaving at most a number index signature.

options.text: `Pick<T, keyof T>`, which copies only the declared properties
options.why: keyof T already includes `string`, so Pick copies the index signature back.

options.text: `{ [K in keyof T as string extends K ? never : number extends K ? never : symbol extends K ? never : K]: T[K] }`
options.why: Only the wide index-signature keys satisfy `string extends K`; literal keys like "id" do not.

explanation: The trick is to reverse the check. For a literal key `"id"`, `string extends "id"` is false, so the key is kept. For the index signature key `string`, `string extends string` is true, so it is remapped to `never` and removed. The same is done for `number` and `symbol` index signatures. Mapping a homomorphic type over `keyof T` sees the index signature keys as `string` and `number`, which is what makes this filter work.
reference: TypeScript Handbook: Key Remapping via as

options.text: `{ c: true }`, because `keyof (A | B)` is only the shared key
options.why: That would be true of mapping over `keyof (A | B)` written out directly, not through a type parameter.

options.text: `{ a: true; b: true; c: true }`, because the keys are merged
options.why: Mapped types never merge union members into one object.

options.text: An error, because a mapped type cannot take a union type argument
options.why: Unions are valid arguments; the question is whether the mapping distributes.

options.text: `{ a: true; c: true } | { b: true; c: true }`
options.why: A homomorphic mapped type distributes over a union type argument, mapping each member separately.

explanation: Homomorphic mapped types (`{ [K in keyof T]: … }` with `T` a type parameter) are distributive over unions: `Mark<A | B>` becomes `Mark<A> | Mark<B>`. Contrast `Omit`, which is not homomorphic in `T` because it maps over `Exclude<keyof T, K>`, and therefore collapses unions to their shared keys.

stem:
Using the naive `DeepPartial`, what is `DeepPartial<{ tags: string[] }>`?

```ts
type DeepPartial<T> = { [K in keyof T]?: DeepPartial<T[K]> };
```

options.text: `{ tags?: string[] }`, because recursion stops at arrays
options.why: Nothing stops the recursion at arrays; the mapped type is applied to `string[]` as well.

options.text: `{ tags?: (string | undefined)[] }`
options.why: Mapping an array type with `?` makes the elements optional, which adds `undefined` to the element type.

options.text: `{ tags?: { [index: number]?: string } }`, an object with optional numeric keys
options.why: Homomorphic mapped types over arrays produce arrays, not plain objects.

options.text: `{ tags?: Partial<string>[] }`, which collapses to `{}` elements
options.why: Primitives pass through a homomorphic mapped type unchanged, so elements stay `string` apart from the added `undefined`.

explanation: The array is mapped too: `DeepPartial<string[]>` adds `?` to each element, which TypeScript represents as `(string | undefined)[]`. That is usually not what you want, since it lets `{ tags: [undefined] }` type-check. Robust versions special-case arrays, for example `T extends (infer U)[] ? DeepPartial<U>[] : …`, and also stop at functions and built-ins like Date.

stem: Which two statements about tuple and array types are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: `[string, number]["length"]` is the literal type `2`
options.why: A fixed tuple records its exact length as a literal type.

options.text: `string[]["length"]` is `number`
options.why: Plain arrays have an unknown length.

options.text: `[string, number?]["length"]` is `2`
options.why: With an optional element the length can be 1 or 2, so it is `1 | 2`.

options.text: `(readonly [1, 2])[number]` is `number`
options.why: Indexing a tuple with `number` gives the union of its element types, `1 | 2`.

options.text: `[string, ...number[]]["length"]` is `1`
options.why: A rest element makes the length unbounded, so it is `number`.

explanation: Tuple `length` types encode how many elements a tuple can have: a literal for fixed tuples, a union for optional elements, and `number` once a rest element appears. Type-level arithmetic tricks, such as counting by building tuples and reading `["length"]`, rely on exactly these rules.

stem: Which three statements about `Awaited` are true? (Choose three.)

options.text: `Awaited<number>` is `number`
options.why: Non-thenable types pass through unchanged, just as `await 42` gives 42.

options.text: `Awaited<{ then(onfulfilled: (value: string) => void): void }>` is `string`
options.why: Awaited unwraps any object with a matching `then` method, not just Promise.

options.text: `Awaited<Promise<string> | number>` is `string | number`
options.why: Awaited distributes over unions, unwrapping each member separately.

options.text: `Awaited<Promise<Promise<1>>>` is `Promise<1>`
options.why: Awaited is recursive, so the result is `1`.

options.text: `ReturnType<() => Promise<boolean>>` is `boolean`
options.why: ReturnType does not unwrap promises; you need `Awaited<ReturnType<…>>` for `boolean`.

explanation: `Awaited<T>` mirrors the runtime behaviour of `await`. It recursively unwraps thenables (any object whose `then` takes an `onfulfilled` callback), passes other types through, and distributes over unions. A common pattern for async function results is `Awaited<ReturnType<typeof fn>>`.
reference: TypeScript 4.5 release notes: The Awaited Type

stem:
Type the union that `Idx` resolves to.

```ts
type Idx = Exclude<keyof [string, number], keyof any[]>;
```
explanation: `keyof [string, number]` contains everything an array has (`number`, `"length"`, `"push"` and so on) plus the tuple's own index keys `"0"` and `"1"`. `keyof any[]` covers the shared array members, so excluding them leaves only the string-literal tuple indexes `"0" | "1"`. Note that they are strings, not numbers, because object keys are strings in JavaScript.
reference: TypeScript Handbook: Keyof Type Operator; Tuple Types
